item.title: Khoa Le joins the group as a PhD student
item.description:
We welcome Khoa Le (Lê Anh Khoa) to the group! Khoa is a PhD student in Mechanical Engineering at Purdue University, and joins us to explore functional and energy materials with computational methods and simulations.

Khoa comes to computation from the laboratory. He studied Materials Science and Engineering, with a double major in Chemistry, at the Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (GIST) in South Korea, where his undergraduate thesis was on high-entropy lanthanide-based perovskites. He has also studied the thin-film fabrication of inorganic semiconductors at Monash University in Australia and, at Purdue, laser-induced biomaterials with Prof. Jingang Li.

Welcome, Khoa!

item.title: Purdue Mechanical Engineering welcomes Piero Canepa as Associate Professor with tenure
item.description:
The School of Mechanical Engineering at Purdue University welcomes its new faculty members in a news story, among them Piero Canepa, who joined Purdue in November 2026 as Associate Professor of Mechanical Engineering with tenure.

The story describes the lab’s research: computational methods that combine materials science, thermodynamics, electrochemistry and supercomputing to discover new materials and molecules, for clean-energy technologies such as battery electrodes, ionic conductors and liquid electrolytes.

We are looking for graduate students and postdocs to join us at Purdue: see Join our team.

item.title: Our first day at Purdue University
item.description:
Today, November 2nd, 2026, is our first day at Purdue University, where the Canepa Research Lab is now part of the School of Mechanical Engineering, as announced in September.

The photo shows the sun of the Visiting Our Solar System model, a scale model of the solar system, in which the sun is about 45 feet across and Earth about six inches. It is dedicated to Purdue alumna Janice Voss, the university’s first female astronaut.

We are looking for graduate students and postdocs to join us at Purdue: see Join our team.

item.title: Two invited talks and a contributed talk at the 250th ECS Meeting in Calgary
item.description:
The group was at the 250th ECS Meeting of the Electrochemical Society, held on October 25–29, 2026, at the BMO Centre in Calgary, Canada.

Piero Canepa gave two invited talks:

  • “Understanding and Mitigating Reactive Interfaces in All-Solid-State Batteries”, on which pairs of solid electrolytes can be stacked into stable bilayer separators for all-solid-state batteries (see our paper on halide bilayer separators).
  • “Finding Active and Inactive Ion Sites in Organic Crystalline Materials for Electrochemical Applications”, on our methods for locating light ions such as lithium and hydrogen in organic crystals (see our paper in Chemical Science).

PhD student Harshan Reddy Gopidi gave a contributed talk, “Theory-Guided Crystal Structure Resolution of β-Li4-o-DHT: A High-Voltage Organic Electrode Material”, on solving the crystal structure of a high-voltage organic electrode material that powder diffraction alone had left unsolved.

The work was carried out with our colleagues in the Energy Storage Research Alliance (ESRA) at Argonne, Oak Ridge and Pacific Northwest National Laboratories, the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, the University of California San Diego and the University of Houston.

item.title: Farewell from the Texas Center for Superconductivity
item.description:
On October 22nd, 2026, colleagues at the Texas Center for Superconductivity (TcSUH) at the University of Houston gathered to bid farewell to Prof. Piero Canepa and Prof. Yan Yao, who are leaving Houston for Purdue University and Columbia University, respectively.

Over cake and flowers, the center thanked both for their research, teaching and service at TcSUH and UH. We are deeply grateful to our colleagues at TcSUH and across the University of Houston for their support and friendship during our years in Houston, and we look forward to continuing our collaborations from our new homes.

The Canepa Research Lab moves to the School of Mechanical Engineering at Purdue University on November 2nd, 2026 (see our earlier announcement). More photos are in Life in the group.

item.title: The Canepa Research Lab is moving to Purdue University
item.description:
We are thrilled to announce that on November 2nd, 2026, the Canepa Research Lab will move from the University of Houston to Purdue University, joining the School of Mechanical Engineering! This is an exciting new chapter for the group, and we can’t wait to continue exploring and designing functional materials in our new home.

Interested in joining us? Potential graduate students and research fellows are invited to visit our Join our team page. All inquiries and applications should be routed to Prof. Canepa at canepa [at] purdue.edu.

item.title: Our perspective on machine learning interatomic potentials for solid-state batteries appears in Chem. Mater.
item.description:
Our perspective “Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials for Modeling Solid-State Batteries” has been published in Chemistry of Materials, DOI: 10.1021/acs.chemmater.6c01051. The work was led by Mgcini Keith Phuthi and Shyue Ping Ong, and brings together researchers from UC San Diego, UC Berkeley, MIT, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Argonne National Laboratory, the National University of Singapore, the University of Houston, and Purdue University.

This work is part of the Energy Storage Research Alliance (ESRA), an Energy Innovation Hub funded by the U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Science, Basic Energy Sciences.

Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) model the potential energy surface of a material at near-first-principles accuracy for a fraction of the cost of density functional theory, which opens up length and time scales that ab initio methods cannot reach. The perspective discusses how MLIPs, and foundation potentials in particular, can predict the key properties of battery materials, from phase stability, ionic conductivity and voltage to mechanical and thermal properties; how they can model interfaces, interphases and reactions; and how they can speed up high-throughput screening and materials discovery. It closes with what the next generation of MLIPs will need, including charge-aware models, long-range interactions and better training data.

The paper can be found here.

item.title: The ESRA all-hands meeting at Argonne National Laboratory
item.description:
On August 26th, 2026, members of the group joined researchers from across the Energy Storage Research Alliance (ESRA) at Argonne National Laboratory for the alliance’s all-hands meeting.

ESRA is an Energy Innovation Hub funded by the U.S. Department of Energy, led by Argonne, which brings together national laboratories and universities to develop the next generation of batteries and energy storage. Our group is part of the alliance’s work on organic and solid-state battery materials, with partners at Argonne, Oak Ridge and Pacific Northwest National Laboratories and several universities (see our talks at the ECS Meeting in Calgary).

item.title: An ARPA-E award to design ultra-strong magnets
item.description:
We are part of a team that has received an award from the U.S. Department of Energy’s Advanced Research Projects Agency–Energy (ARPA-E), in its MAGNITO program (Magnetic Acceleration Generating New Innovations and Tactical Outcomes), for the project “Motifs to Magnets: Ultra-strong Magnets Through Wyckoff and Lego-like Design”, together with Prashun Gorai at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute and Boniface Fokwa at the University of California, Riverside.

Permanent magnets drive electric motors and generators, from electric vehicles to wind turbines, and the strongest ones rely on rare-earth elements. MAGNITO seeks permanent magnets stronger than any known material. As its title says, our project will look for them by design: assembling crystal structures from structural motifs, described by the positions their atoms occupy (their Wyckoff positions), like Lego bricks. Piero Canepa and the group will study and discover new strong permanent magnets with multiscale methods.

item.title: Hoa My Nguyễn joins the group to study Zr–Au hydrides
item.description:
We welcome Hoa My (Mimi) Nguyễn to the group! Mimi, a senior undergraduate in Chemical Engineering at the University of Houston, joins us to work on Zr–Au hydrides, as part of a collaborative project with the Brgoch lab in the Department of Chemistry. Using first-principles calculations, Mimi will study the thermodynamic stability of these hydrides.

Welcome, Mimi!

item.title: Our sodium-battery paper wins the 2024 IOM3 Vanadium Award
item.description:
Our paper “Obtaining V2(PO4)3 by sodium extraction from single-phase NaxV2(PO4)3 (1 < x < 3) positive electrode materials”, published in Nature Materials, has received the 2024 Vanadium Award (Retrospective) of the Institute of Materials, Minerals and Mining (IOM3), among its 2025 Awards and Prizes. The medal was presented at the IOM3 Awards Day ceremony in London on December 4, 2025, by IOM3 President Christine Blackmore.

Sponsored and selected by the Vanadium International Technical Committee (Vanitec), the award recognizes the most outstanding paper in the metallurgy and technology of vanadium and its alloys. The paper was written by Sunkyu Park, Ziliang Wang, Kriti Choudhary, Jean-Noël Chotard, Dany Carlier, François Fauth, Piero Canepa, Laurence Croguennec and Christian Masquelier, together with our colleagues at LRCS in Amiens and ICMCB in Bordeaux, France.

item.title: Michael Ho and Folasade Adegoju join the group for the summer
item.description:

Folasade Adegoju, from B. F. Terry High School, joins us as a high-school summer student through the American Chemical Society’s Project SEED, which gives students from economically disadvantaged backgrounds a paid summer of research in an academic lab.

item.title: The Research Corporation for Science Advancement funds our research
item.description:
Our group received support from Research Corporation For Science Advancement for a research project titled “Autonomous Discovery of Single-phase High-Entropy Transition Metal Chalcogenides”. This work is in collaboration with Shijing Sun at the University of Washington and Zak Al Balushi at UC Berkeley. We consider this a significant achievement, particularly during these uncertain times for federal funding.

Research Corporation For Science Advancement is a foundation providing catalytic funding for innovative scientific research and the development of academic scientists since 1912.

item.title: The Welch Foundation funds our research
item.description:
Our group received support from The Welch Foundation for a research project titled “Exploring Links between Vibrational and Configurational Entropies in Complex Oxides via First-Principles and Machine Learning.” This is a significant achievement, particularly during these uncertain times for federal funding.

The Welch Foundation supports fundamental chemical research at educational institutions within the state of Texas. A research grant provides a minimum of $100,000 per year in funding to support research in chemistry by a full-time regular faculty member with tenure or on tenure-track who serves as principal investigator. Applications are restricted to universities, colleges, or other educational institutions located within the state of Texas and also listed as an educational institution by the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board.

item.title: Our sodium-battery work in Nature Materials is featured in Science
item.description: Our research recently published in Nature Materials, “Obtaining V2(PO4)3 by sodium extraction from single-phase NaxV2(PO4)3 (1 < x < 3) positive electrode materials” (Nat. item.title: Our new sodium-battery material in Nature Materials makes the news
item.description:
Our paper “Obtaining V2(PO4)3 by sodium extraction from single-phase NaxV2(PO4)3 (1 < x < 3) positive electrode materials”, published in Nature Materials (DOI: 10.1038/s41563-024-02023-7) with our colleagues at LRCS in Amiens and ICMCB in Bordeaux, France, has been covered widely in the press, in English and other languages, including through a University of Houston press release. Ziliang Wang worked on the paper as a member of our group. The new single-phase cathode material raises the operating voltage of a sodium-ion battery from 3.37 V to 3.70 V, increasing its theoretical energy density by about 15%, from 396 to 458 Wh kg−1.

item.title: Piero Canepa and Yan Yao talk about better batteries on Houston Public Media
item.description:
Piero Canepa and Yan Yao, then of the University of Houston’s Cullen College of Engineering, were interviewed on Houston Matters, Houston Public Media’s daily talk show on its NPR station, about how UH hopes to help build better, longer-lasting batteries. Listen to the segment:

The conversation was about the University of Houston’s part in the Energy Storage Research Alliance (ESRA), an Energy Innovation Hub funded by the U.S. Department of Energy that UH joined this month. Yan Yao leads the UH project, with Piero Canepa as co-principal investigator, combining the experiments of the Yao group with our computations to design solid-state batteries.

item.title: Piero Canepa gives a Pint of Science talk on sodium batteries in Houston
item.description:
On May 15th, 2024, Piero Canepa gave an invited talk, “Moving Beyond Lithium-ion Batteries: the Rise of the Sodium Rechargeable Battery”, at Pint of Science in Houston, at True Anomaly Brewing Co. Pint of Science is a festival that brings researchers to pubs and bars to share their work with the public.

The talk explained why sodium batteries are a promising, more sustainable alternative to lithium-ion batteries, and how our research on batteries helps design them.

item.title: Our work on lithium and sodium ion exchange in layered oxides appears in Nature Materials
item.description:
Our collaborative paper “Uncovering the Predictive Pathways of Lithium and Sodium Interchange in Layered Oxides” is out in Nature Materials, with Weihang Xie from our group among its authors.

Ion exchange, swapping the sodium in a material for lithium or the other way round, is a powerful way to make metastable electrode materials that cannot be synthesized directly, but it usually needs a large excess of lithium, and its reaction pathways were unclear. Using layered oxides as model materials, the study shows that the number of vacancies, and the preference for lithium that comes with it, decides which exchange pathways are open. With this understanding, the team made NayCoO2 from LixCoO2, and Li0.94CoO2 back from NayCoO2, in solutions with as little as one lithium for every 1,000 sodium ions, by an electrochemically assisted exchange. The results open new routes to the predictive synthesis of electrode materials and to the separation of lithium from sodium.

item.title: Our solid-electrolyte paper wins the 2023 Chemistry of Materials Lectureship and Best Paper Award
item.description:
Our paper “Devil is in the Defects: Electronic Conductivity in Solid Electrolytes”, published in Chemistry of Materials in 2021, has received the 2023 Chemistry of Materials Lectureship and Best Paper Award. The award was presented at the Chemistry of Materials Lectureship and Best Paper Award Symposium of the ACS Spring 2024 National Meeting in New Orleans (March 17–21, 2024).

The award recognizes the authors of an article published in Chemistry of Materials in the previous two years that has had an outstanding influence across materials chemistry. The paper was written by Prashun Gorai, Theodosios Famprikis, Baltej Singh, Vladan Stevanović and Piero Canepa, together with our colleagues at the Colorado School of Mines and Delft University of Technology.

item.title: We took part in the Energy Day Festival in Houston
item.description:
On October 21st, 2023, Piero Canepa and Abhishek Panchal volunteered at the Energy Day Festival in Sam Houston Park, Downtown Houston. Organized by the Consumer Energy Education Foundation, Energy Day is a free family festival with hands-on exhibits and demonstrations that teach students and their families about the many forms of energy and spark their interest in science, technology, engineering, and math.

At our table, children built batteries out of fruit, wiring apples and limes together with alligator clips, and learned how the chemistry inside a battery turns into electricity, the same chemistry our group studies to design better batteries.

See more photos of the group in Life in the group.

item.title: Our zirconia-free NaSICON paper in the Journal of Materials Chemistry A collection celebrating RSC Fellows
item.description:
Our paper “Zirconia-free NaSICON solid electrolyte materials for sodium all-solid-state batteries”, J. Mater. Chem. A 11, 23233–23242 (2023), is part of the Royal Society of Chemistry’s collection “Celebrating the scientific accomplishments of RSC Fellows” in the Journal of Materials Chemistry A. Piero Canepa is a Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry.

NaSICON solid electrolytes, Na1+xZr2SixP3−xO12 (0 ≤ x ≤ 3), are widely studied for all-solid-state sodium batteries, but as synthesized they always contain monoclinic zirconia (ZrO2) as the main impurity, which may lower the Na-ion conductivity of the electrolyte layer. By engineering the quantity of zirconium precursors, we made zirconia-free NaSICON, as revealed by synchrotron X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy and density functional theory simulations. Its total ionic conductivity at room temperature is about 3.49 mS cm−1, with a bulk conductivity of about 10.05 mS cm−1, which makes it an excellent Na-ion conductor for all-solid-state batteries.

The paper was written by Aaron J. K. Tieu, Eunike Mahayoni, Yuheng Li, Zeyu Deng, François Fauth, Jean-Noël Chotard, Vincent Seznec, Stefan Adams, Christian Masquelier and Piero Canepa.

item.title: An invited talk at the International Battery Association meeting in Bled
item.description:
Piero Canepa gave an invited talk, “Millisecond Ion-Transport in Mixed Polyanion Battery Materials”, at the International Battery Association meeting IBA 2022, held on October 2–7, 2022, in Bled, Slovenia.

The talk was on how mixing silicate and phosphate groups speeds up sodium ions in the NASICON solid electrolyte Na1+xZr2SixP3−xO12, for all-solid-state sodium batteries, which we mapped with more than 2,000 kinetic Monte Carlo simulations, each following the ions’ motion over milliseconds (see our paper in Nature Communications with Zeyu Deng, Tara P. Mishra, Aaron J. K. Tieu and colleagues).
